newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's 98 budget draft could be ready this month.
newsitem.headline: Spain's 98 budget draft could be ready this month.

text.p: Spain has begun work on the 1998 budget and may present a first draft before the August holiday period, Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato said on Tuesday.
The one-year-old centre-right government has pledged to reduce Spain's budget deficit as a share of gross domestic product to 2.5 percent in 1998 from three percent forecast this year.

"The budget draft is at a preliminary phase...we are now having talks. I expect the cabinet will be made familiar with the budget draft before the August holiday," he told journalists after an earlier meeting with regional economy officials.

The government does not expect to change the main characteristics of its economic policy, which has helped get Spain into sufficient shape to join the first wave of Europe's single currency, scheduled for 1999.
"The budget law and government economy policy will aim to stabilise the current economic situation," Rato said.

Public deficit reduction without increased fiscal pressure, economic liberalisation in high-growth sectors and incentives for small- and medium-sized companies will be main points of the 1998 budget, Rato added.
"The Exchequer Secretary (Juan Costa) is working on (the idea) of not increasing the fiscal burden," Rato said.
Spain's convergence plan predicts a 5.9 percent increase in total public revenues and of 4.7 percent in total expenditures in 1998.
Public investment, which fell around 14 percent in 1997, could show a pick-up in 1998, Rato said.
"There is scope for public investment to recover at a moderate rate during 1998," Rato said, adding the government intends to use a mix of public and private capital to finance new projects.

But he did not mention other spending increases, despite recent press reports that the government's Catalan regional ally was asking for 200 billion pesetas more to finance public health, and better funding for education and housing.
Healthier growth should provide some help. Gross domestic product (GDP), initially expected to be around three percent this year, is seen climbing to 3.2 percent in 1998.
The Spanish economy is growing at an substantial rate with sustained growth in employment, as data constantly show.
"In 1997 we will be a little bit above forecasts but I can't add anything more before we present the budget," Rato said.
Also seen as key to the new budget is inflation, considered under control, allowing the deficit to be tamed without sacrificing economic growth.
"The economy is not overheating," Rato said. "Consumption is growing, but at a moderate rate. Monetary policy is working in a effective and efficient way," he added.
After May's consumer price index rose 1.5 percent year- on-year, the government expects to end 1997 with inflation at 2.0 percent.
